name: Gresham's Law
meaning: When two coins are legal tender at the same face value but one contains more valuable metal, people spend the inferior coin and hoard, melt, or export the valuable one, so over time only the inferior money keeps circulating.
mechanism: It is rational self-interest under a binding constraint. A legal-tender law, or a fixed official exchange rate, forces both coins to be accepted at the same face value. So a rational holder pays debts with the coin whose metal is worth less and keeps (or melts, or sells abroad) the coin whose metal is worth more. The economist Robert Mundell's precise restatement makes the condition explicit: bad money drives out good only if they exchange for the same price.

examples.text: After Henry VIII and Edward VI debased England's coinage, full-weight silver coins were hoarded, melted, or shipped abroad while the clipped and debased coins circulated: the very phenomenon Gresham described to the Crown.

When the United States removed silver from dimes and quarters in 1965, the older 90%-silver coins (now worth more as metal than as money) were hoarded and vanished from circulation, a clean modern instance of the law.

Under late-stage hyperinflation the pattern flips: once the bad money is nearly worthless and no longer effectively forced as legal tender, people refuse it and revert to commodity or foreign money (the boundary the law runs into (see Thiers' law)).

variants.name: Thiers' law
variants.text: The reverse, named by Peter Bernholz after Adolphe Thiers: good money drives out bad once the bad money becomes nearly worthless and legal-tender enforcement collapses (Gresham's law with its scope condition removed).

variants.name: Gresham–Copernicus law
variants.text: An alternate name marking that Copernicus stated the principle around 1519, before Gresham: one of several earlier statements (Oresme, and Aristophanes in 405 BC) that make it a Stigler's-law case.

variants.name: The market for lemons
variants.text: George Akerlof's information-asymmetry cousin: when buyers cannot tell good goods from bad, quality sellers exit and bad goods dominate (the bad driving out the good by hidden quality rather than by legal par).

whyItMatters: It is a foundational result in monetary economics, explaining why good coin disappears under debasement and why fixed exchange arrangements leak. Understood with its scope condition, it also inoculates against the loose analogies ('bad journalism drives out good') that borrow its slogan without its mechanism.

working.text: the law only bites where a legal-tender rule or fixed rate forces two monies to trade at the same value; that constraint is the whole engine.

working.lead: Expect the good money to hide
working.text: when one form of money is worth more than its face value, assume it will be hoarded, melted, or exported rather than spent.
'bad X drives out good X' for software or culture usually lacks the forced-par mechanism, so treat those as rhetoric, not the law.

limits: Gresham's law holds only within a bounded scope: it requires a binding legal-tender law or fixed exchange ratio forcing acceptance at par. Remove that constraint and the law fails and can reverse, Thiers' law, as it does in hyperinflations where people abandon the bad money entirely. Mundell's qualifier ('if they exchange for the same price') is the true condition, and dropping it makes the 'law' false. It is also endlessly over-extended by analogy to non-monetary domains, where the mechanism does not apply.
misreadings: It does not say bad things always beat good things in general. It is a specific claim about money under forced par. Outside that constraint it does not hold and can even run backwards, and the popular 'bad drives out good' analogies mostly borrow the words without the mechanism.
origin: Named after Sir Thomas Gresham (1519–1579), a financier to the English Crown who observed good coin disappearing after the Tudor debasements, though the term 'Gresham's law' was coined by Henry Dunning Macleod in 1858, and the principle had been stated earlier by Copernicus, Oresme, and even Aristophanes' play The Frogs (c. 405 BC), making it a textbook case of Stigler's law of eponymy.

sources.text: Macleod, H. D. (1858). “The Elements of Political Economy.” London: Longman, Brown, Green, Longmans and Roberts. — the book that NAMED the law after Gresham. Gresham never stated it, and Macleod’s attribution is the source of the name rather than of the idea — which is why this entry is also in the misattributed set.
Gresham's law, Wikipedia. — the statement, Mundell's qualifier, the Macleod naming, and the earlier statements by Copernicus, Oresme, and Aristophanes.
Thiers' law, Wikipedia. — the reverse case under collapsed legal tender.
Coinage Act of 1965, Wikipedia. — the removal of silver and the disappearance of silver coins from US circulation.
